questions.label: Walk-in
questions.prompt: A patient from 1923 walks into your office. What's your first question?

options.label: "Tell me what brought you here in your own words."
"What's the loudest thing you noticed on the way in?"
"Tell me one thing that's the same as the year you left."
"Sit. I'll explain the world as it is now, in a moment."

questions.label: The new language
questions.prompt: The patient keeps using a word that doesn't exist yet. You...

options.label: Guess what they mean from how they say it
Ask them to define it as if teaching a child
Reflect the word back and watch their eyes
Name a modern word that almost fits

questions.label: The 'cure'
questions.prompt: They ask what medicine cures loneliness. You...

options.label: Tell them honestly: it doesn't, but it gets quieter
Tell them about a place in their century that helped
Suggest one small ritual, every morning, for a week
Imagine their answer with them out loud

questions.label: Letter home
questions.prompt: They want to write a letter to someone they left behind. You...

options.label: Help them write it in their own handwriting
Gently edit out what they don't mean yet
Wait until the silence in them settles first
Suggest they keep it folded until tomorrow

questions.label: The tablet
questions.prompt: You show them a tablet screen. They ask what it costs the soul. You...

options.label: Talk about what it gives before what it takes
Warn them about the part that's almost free
Ask them to list one thing it replaces
Wonder aloud what their century would have invented instead

questions.label: Future patient
questions.prompt: A patient from 2125 arrives next. Your first instinct is to...

options.label: Prepare by rereading everything I've learned
Ask the 1923 patient to stay and translate
Listen longer than I plan to talk
Imagine their first breath on our air

questions.label: Silence
questions.prompt: There's a long silence in the session. You...

options.label: Hold the silence and trust what it's doing
Name the silence so they can choose what it is
Offer a small question that opens a door sideways
Tell them a story about silence from another era

questions.label: Goodbye
questions.prompt: It's time for them to return. The room feels heavy. You...

options.label: Make a small ritual of the leaving — a sentence, a cup of tea
Ground them in the next concrete thing they'll see
Tell them a true thing that took you years to learn
Ask to follow, just to the door, just to the street

questions.label: Case note
questions.prompt: In your private case note, you write...

options.label: What they told me, almost verbatim
What I noticed about myself in the session
The theory that fits, even if it isn't mine
A metaphor I can return to next time

questions.label: Office hours
questions.prompt: After they leave, your office hours feel different. You...

options.label: Close the books and walk the long way home
Research everything you assumed but didn't check
Sit with what happened, without trying to use it
Document the room's exact temperature and light

archetypes.label: Counselor
archetypes.tagline: Steady, attuned, and willing to sit in silence longer than anyone else.
archetypes.blindSpot: Empathic attunement can become emotional enmeshment when the patient leaves.

archetypes.label: Historian
archetypes.tagline: Curious about the smallest detail and what the patient assumed was ordinary.
archetypes.blindSpot: Fascination with context can delay the moment the patient actually needed a word.

archetypes.label: Storyteller
archetypes.tagline: Reaches for a metaphor that lets the patient finish the sentence themselves.
archetypes.blindSpot: A good story can outrun the patient's actual question.

archetypes.label: Scientist
archetypes.tagline: Asks for definitions, tests hypotheses, and refuses to guess in the dark.
archetypes.blindSpot: Method can become a wall when the patient needs to be believed, not studied.

archetypes.label: Mystic
archetypes.tagline: Hears the silence as a room of its own and treats it like a co-therapist.
archetypes.blindSpot: Wonder can be its own avoidance of the small concrete thing the patient came in for.
